questions.explain: Lock-in is a spectrum of switching costs, and data gravity — multi-terabyte databases taking weeks to move — is the dominant cost, existing on every platform including on-premises.
options: Data gravity: multi-terabyte databases take weeks to move — the dominant cost
The price of the managed service
The color of the cloud console
The number of availability zones
questions.q: What is the dominant component of switching cost (lock-in) in practice?

questions.explain: The classic over-engineering is a database abstraction layer hiding which cloud SQL Server runs on — it must be maintained forever, lags native capabilities, and is tested far less than what it replaces.
options: Infrastructure as code
Migration-based deployments
A custom database abstraction layer hiding which cloud the SQL Server runs on
Using standard engine features
questions.q: What is the chapter's 'abstraction layer trap'?

questions.explain: The three questions: what does the feature replace (price the build alternative honestly), how deep does it reach into the application (prefer shallow lock-in), and what is the actual exit scenario (with names and dates).
options: Is it the cheapest option? Is it fashionable? Does the vendor have a nice logo?
What does it replace? How deep does it reach into the application? What is the actual exit scenario?
Can it run on-premises? Is it open source? Is it free?
Does it support Kubernetes? Is it serverless? Is it AI-powered?
questions.q: What is the chapter's three-question framework for deciding whether a proprietary feature is worth the lock-in?

questions.explain: The chapter calls this 80% of practical portability: every SQL Server everywhere can restore a native backup, so keep backup chains in standard formats in object storage you control.
options: Running everything on VMs
Keeping native backups in standard formats in object storage you control
Avoiding all managed features
Writing your own replication
questions.q: What single practice is '80% of practical portability'?

questions.explain: The exit plan is a document, not an architecture: portable artifacts, estimated approach, measured (not estimated) data-transfer time, and explicitly listed deep-lock-in dependencies — reviewed annually.
options: The exit plan is a document listing portable artifacts, measured transfer times, and deep-lock-in dependencies — reviewed annually
A second active cloud running at all times
A legal contract forbidding lock-in
An abstraction layer over everything
questions.q: What form should an exit plan take, and how often is it reviewed?

title: Chapter 28: Avoiding Vendor Lock-In Without Over-Engineering
